package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed via multiple vectors, not a package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: Fickle Stealer is a modular, Rust-based infostealer distributed via multiple attack chains (malicious documents, PowerShell scripts, and packed executables). It performs credential and data theft from browsers, wallets, and applications, exfiltrates sensitive files, evades analysis, and self-deletes to avoid detection.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Drops a copy of WmiMgmt.msc and a fake WmiMgmt.msc to C:\Windows\System32 and C:\Windows\System32\en-US, abuses ActiveX to open a web browser, sets up an HttpListener, configures exclusions for the stealer, and downloads/executes the stealer with elevated privileges.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During preparatory work, the script bypasses UAC by abusing a fake WmiMgmt.msc, launches a local web server, configures malware exclusions, and downloads/executes the stealer with elevated privileges.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: UAC bypass, privilege escalation, and execution of untrusted code are classic malware behaviors.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts should not bypass UAC or execute arbitrary binaries with elevated privileges.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, IT automation may use UAC bypass for legitimate software deployment, but not with fake system files or web server tricks.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Creates a new scheduled task to execute engine.ps1 after 15 minutes.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the script establishes persistence by scheduling a delayed execution of the next-stage payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malware often uses scheduled tasks for persistence and delayed execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers rarely schedule hidden tasks to run additional scripts after a delay.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Enumerates .exe files in user directories (C:\Users\, D:\, E:\, F:\), runs inject.ps1 to inject shellcode that executes u.ps1 from the internet, and logs injected file paths (base64-encoded) to C:\Users\Public\prepares.dat.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the script searches for executables, injects shellcode to re-execute the initial payload, and tracks infected files.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Injecting shellcode into executables is a hallmark of malware propagation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts do not inject code into unrelated executables or maintain infection logs.

execution_context.file_location: tgmes.ps1 (PowerShell script, dropped to Temp with random name)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Sends victim information (country, city, IP, OS version, computer/user name) and status messages to attacker's Telegram bot, then deletes itself.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the script exfiltrates system and victim data to a remote Telegram bot and self-deletes to evade detection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating system info to Telegram and immediate self-deletion are classic anti-forensics and C2 behaviors.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts do not send sensitive system info to external messaging platforms.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Packer replaces the __cinit function in a legitimate executable to allocate memory, decrypt, and execute the stealer payload in memory before WinMain.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At process initialization, the packer executes malicious code before the main application logic, decrypts the payload, and runs it in memory.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Code execution before WinMain and in-memory payload unpacking are advanced evasion techniques.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications do not modify their initialization routines to run hidden code.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Checks for debuggers (BeingDebugged flag), blacklisted process names, loaded analysis DLLs, virtual machine artifacts, hardware IDs, and suspicious usernames. Exits or shows fake error if analysis detected.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the payload performs multiple anti-analysis checks and terminates if analysis is detected.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Comprehensive anti-analysis logic is a strong indicator of sophisticated malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not evade analysis or terminate in the presence of debuggers.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Collects files and credentials from browsers, wallets, plugins, and applications; parses browser databases for cookies, history, and login data; copies files to Temp, compresses and base64-encodes them, and sends to C2 server. Also takes a screenshot and deletes itself.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the payload steals sensitive data, exfiltrates it to the C2 server, takes a screenshot, and self-deletes.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Mass data theft, credential exfiltration, and self-deletion are core infostealer behaviors.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not harvest or exfiltrate user data, nor does it self-delete after execution.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At the end of execution, the stealer schedules its own deletion to remove traces.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-deletion is a classic anti-forensics technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate applications do not delete themselves after execution.

attack_chain.action: Initial delivery via malicious document or downloader (VBA macro, link, or executable) downloads and executes u.ps1/bypass.ps1.
u.ps1/bypass.ps1 bypasses UAC, configures exclusions, and downloads/executes the stealer with elevated privileges.
u.ps1 schedules engine.ps1 to run after a delay for persistence.
engine.ps1 enumerates executables, injects shellcode via inject.ps1 to propagate infection, and logs infected files.
tgmes.ps1 exfiltrates victim info and status to Telegram bot, then self-deletes.
Packed executable unpacks and executes the stealer payload in memory before main application logic.
Stealer payload performs anti-analysis checks and terminates if analysis is detected.
Stealer payload collects and exfiltrates sensitive data, takes a screenshot, and deletes itself.

behavioral_signatures: PowerShell scripts that drop or execute fake system files (e.g., WmiMgmt.msc)
UAC bypass via Mock Trusted Directories or ActiveX/HttpListener abuse
Creation of scheduled tasks for delayed script execution
Enumeration and injection into user executables
Frequent outbound connections to Telegram APIs or suspicious C2 servers
In-memory unpacking of payloads before WinMain
Anti-analysis checks (debugger, VM, username, hardware ID)
Mass file and credential exfiltration from browsers, wallets, and plugins
Self-deletion of scripts and binaries after execution
file_indicators: u.ps1, bypass.ps1, engine.ps1, inject.ps1, tgmes.ps1 in Temp or user directories
Randomly named PowerShell scripts in Temp
Packed executables with modified __cinit or initialization routines
network_indicators: Outbound connections to Telegram bot APIs
Exfiltration of compressed, base64-encoded JSON data
Frequent short-lived connections during data theft
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for PowerShell scripts that drop or execute fake system files, abuse UAC, or create scheduled tasks. Detect enumeration and injection into user executables, and watch for outbound connections to Telegram or known C2 IPs. Look for mass file access in browser, wallet, and plugin directories, and self-deleting binaries/scripts. Correlate anti-analysis checks and in-memory unpacking with suspicious process trees. Flag compressed, base64-encoded JSON exfiltration patterns.
